title: metric-led-pricing-narrative-and-token-evidence
content:
Purpose

This is a working messaging brief and competitive-notes bundle focused on: metric framing (how to talk about units of value for different buyer profiles), a concise ‘why token pricing’ narrative, practical tier prototypes, and discount/negotiation guardrails. Goal: give GTM (growth, sales, CS) a short script + tests to validate with accounts and a rubric for allowed discounts.

Key hypothesis (one line)

Framing pricing around token-based usage + a small set of derived unit metrics (active sessions, embeddings/day, concurrent capacity) reduces buyer confusion, maps cleanly to engineering tradeoffs (latency/cost), and lets us optimize around predictable contract economics for Dedicated/Private.

Narrative pillars (short)

1) Metric alignment: charge for the thing customers actually consume (tokens) while surfacing derived metrics in product UX for predictability (requests/min, avg tokens/request).
2) Engineering fidelity: tokens directly map to GPU cycles and caching behavior — token pricing connects value to cost and enables honest optimization suggestions (batching, KV cache).
3) Choice & predictability: tiers bundle token budgets with capacity guarantees (dedicated QPS/latency) so customers trade simplicity vs unit cost.
4) Trust & transparency: publish per-model token cost ranges and typical per-feature unit economics so customers can estimate bill with confidence.

Why token pricing — short script for sales/marketing

- “Tokens are the canonical unit of compute for modern models — they reflect what actually drives cost on the GPU. Charging by tokens lets you scale predictably as usage rises and captures the primary cost driver across text generation, chat, and embeddings.”
- “We pair tokens with derived metrics in the console (tokens per request, average sequence length, embeddings per minute). That makes it easy to forecast spend without exposing billing math to end users.”

One-paragraph elevator pitch (for decks)

We price by tokens because tokens are the most direct measure of model compute and therefore the cleanest way to align customer value with system cost. Token pricing simplifies comparisons (same unit across models/features), lets developers optimize their prompts and caching to reduce spend, and allows Redwood to provide predictable tiered SLAs by coupling token budgets with capacity guarantees.

Competitive framing notes (short bullets)

- Vendor A (closed-stack API): flat per-request plus tiers — easy to understand but opaque to model size and sequence-length risk; customers frequently face surprise overages when moving from dev to prod.
- Vendor B (per-second billing on dedicated inference): good for latency-sensitive cases but penalizes short, bursty workloads and makes multi-model routing harder to price.
- Vendor C (feature-based bundles, e.g., ‘chat seats’): attractive for PLG SMBs but hard to scale to high-throughput workloads and poor fit for heavy embedding workloads.

How we position against them

- Against A: emphasize predictability + transparency (per-model token cost bands + usage simulator in console).
- Against B: show examples where token pricing rewards batching/caching and lowers unit costs for high-throughput apps.
- Against C: offer a simple SMB starter tier that mimics ‘seats’ but clearly shows the token budget behind it (translation layer for buyers used to seats).

Tier prototypes (recommended starting set — names are placeholders)

1) Starter (PLG-friendly)
- Who: small teams, prototypes
- Pricing anchor: small monthly token bundle (e.g., 10M tokens/mo) + pay-as-you-go overage
- UX: simple dashboard, quick sandbox models, no SLA
- Why: low barrier and maps to short prototypes and low concurrency

2) Growth (scale apps)
- Who: product teams moving to production
- Pricing anchor: larger bundle (e.g., 150M tokens/mo) + discounted unit overage, modest committed discount (10–20%)
- UX: per-route dashboards, recommendations for batching/quantization
- Why: customers want predictable spend and basic performance guarantees

3) Dedicated (SLA & reserved capacity)
- Who: companies with steady throughput needs
- Pricing anchor: commit to tokens + reserved GPU capacity; price expressed as tokens/mo + fixed infra fee
- SLA: p99 latency target, dedicated pool sizing, rollouts support
- Why: predictable latency and unit economics for scale customers

4) Private / Enterprise
- Who: regulated / on-prem
- Pricing anchor: license + deployment fee + tokens (meter or true-up)
- Negotiation levers: multi-year discounts, custom capacity profiles, dedicated SRE hours

Discounting and negotiation guardrails (practical)

- Standard discount bands by ARR or committed tokens: 0% < $25k ARR; 10% for $25–100k; 20%+ for >$100k with multi-year commitment. These are starting points — S&M may escalate with Legal/RevOps approval.
- Concessions allowed without approvals: one-time free onboarding credits up to 2 months of Starter tier tokens, onboarding SRE up to 10 hours.
- Concessions requiring approval: capacity-related credits, model-specific token rebates, multi-year opt-outs.
- Demo account rules: sandbox always free but limited tokens; extended evaluation (90 days) requires a signed MSA or PO to protect cost.

Negotiation scripts (short)

- If customer asks for lower unit price: "We can reduce your unit price with a committed token bucket — how much predictable monthly usage can you guarantee? Committing lets us size reserved capacity and pass you a lower unit cost."
- If customer wants seat-like simplicity: "We can map your seat count to an internal token budget and show a simple per-seat monthly charge, but we’ll surface token usage in the console for forecasting and potential optimization."

Sales toolkit (quick practical items)

- ROI calculator (spreadsheet) showing: token budget, average tokens/req, expected monthly tokens = requests * avg tokens, projected bill across Starter/Growth/Dedicated. (linked artifact: price-simulations repo)
- Short demo flow: 1) create sandbox with 5M tokens, 2) show console forecast, 3) enable model trace to show per-token cost distribution, 4) propose Growth bundle.
- Objection templates: expense justification, security/regulatory questions (point to Dedicated/Private with audit features), and overage fear (show burst protection + alerts).

Acceptance criteria for tier migration (internal rubric)

- Starter -> Growth: sustained >60% consumption of Starter tokens for 6 weeks or regular >=5% week-over-week growth in monthly tokens.
- Growth -> Dedicated: stable monthly token demand above Growth bundle for 3 months and requirements for p99 latency/throughput guarantees.

Validation experiments (quick A/B tests)

1) Console visibility experiment: show derived metrics (tokens/request) vs not in sign-up flow — measure conversion to Growth plan and churn at 90 days.
2) Pricing wording test: "tokens" vs "compute units" vs "requests" — test NPS and willingness-to-pay in trial cohort.
3) Discount elasticity: offer 10% vs 15% vs 20% on 12-month commits for a matched group; measure lift in ARR and net present value.

Competitive evidence snippets to include in sales enablement

- Case: onboarding a mid-market SaaS that moved from per-seat to tokens — 35% cost reduction after enabling KV caching + prompt-level trimming.
- Case: e-commerce bot with unpredictable peak traffic that moved to Dedicated token bucket + burst policy and saw 55% fewer timeouts during promotions.

Open questions and things to validate with customers

- How intuitive is the token concept to non-technical procurement? (need 3 field interviews with finance buyers)
- For vendors using per-second billing, which customer segments prefer that and why? (SRE/infra-driven customers?)
- Is there appetite for hybrid billing (flat infra fee + tokens) for larger enterprises? (test with 2 pilots)

Action items (owner initials)

- Marcus: build a simplified ROI spreadsheet template and link into demo flow (due 2025-01-20).
- Leila: draft a short one-pager for finance buyers that translates tokens -> expected monthly spend by use case (gen chat, embeddings) (due 2025-01-24).
- Jonas: run the console visibility A/B experiment with 200 trial accounts (start 2025-01-15).
- Ava: synthesize 3 seller scripts for Deal Desk review and finalize discount guardrails (due 2025-02-05).

Notes to reviewers

This is intentionally concise and prescriptive — the aim is to get a repeatable, testable set of narratives in the hands of sellers and product-marketing quickly. Expect iterations after the first two pilots.
